item.title: Probability Distributions - Multinomial Variables
item.description:
2.2 Multinomial Variables

A multinomila variable can be in any of \(K\) states instead of just \(2\) (in case of a binary variable). For example, a multinomial variable having \(K=5\) states can be represented as \(x=(0,0,1,0,0)^T\) where it is in a state where \(x_3=1\). This vector will satisfy \(\sum_{k=1}^K = 1\). If we denote the probability of \(x_k=1\) by \(\mu_k\), the distribution of \(x\) is given as:

\[\begin{align} p(x|\mu) = \prod_{k=1}^{K} \mu_k^{x_k} \end{align}\]

where \(\mu = (\mu_1, \mu_2, ..., \mu_k)^T\) and \(\mu_k \geq 0\) and \(\sum_{k}\mu_k = 1\). This distribution can be considered as the generalization of bernoulli distribution for more than \(2\) outcomes. This distribution is normalized as (only one of the \(x_k=1\) for all \(x\)):
